subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Discuss the effect of catalyst on the kinetics of chemical reaction with diagram.

mark_split.label: What a catalyst does not change

verification.note: Unit 4 (Chemical Kinetics) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.73-76, which prints the question and a model answer. The 2+2+2+2 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK ERROR (book p.75, LAQ 4): the printed answer defines a catalyst as "a substance which increase the speed of reaction without involving in the reaction". That is wrong. A catalyst DOES take part: it forms an intermediate with a reactant and is released again when the products form. What is true is that it is not CONSUMED, and that it is recovered chemically unchanged at the end. NCERT's wording, a substance that alters the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change, is used on this card. BOOK GAP on the same answer: the printed answer stops after "decrease the activation energy hence increases the rate". It never says that a catalyst does NOT change ΔH, that it lowers the forward and reverse activation energies by the SAME amount, and that it therefore leaves the equilibrium constant and the equilibrium yield unchanged and only shortens the time taken to reach equilibrium. Those are added, because they are the half of this topic a board question most often depends on. FIGURE SCOPE: the question says "with diagram", not "draw a neat labelled diagram", so the diagram step carries NO marks and the whole 2+2+2+2 split sits on the four written steps.

steps.label: What a catalyst is
lines: A catalyst is a substance that alters the
rate of a chemical reaction without itself
undergoing any permanent chemical
change.
It does take part in the reaction: it forms
an intermediate with a reactant and is
released again when the products form.
So it is not used up, and it is recovered
unchanged at the end.
A small amount is enough, because the
same catalyst is used again and again.
steps.why: The word permanent is what makes the definition correct. A catalyst that took no part at all could not change anything; it does react, but every step that consumes it is followed by a step that returns it, so the amount present at the end is the amount present at the start.
common_mistakes: Writing that a catalyst does not take part in the reaction. It takes part and is then regenerated; only a permanent change is ruled out.
Writing that a catalyst is used up slowly. If it were, it would be a reactant, not a catalyst.
steps.memory_tip: Takes part, then is released again. Not consumed, and recovered unchanged.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the definition, then the sentence that it is regenerated. The second is the one most answers leave out.

steps.label: The new reaction path
lines: A catalyst provides a different path from
the reactants to the products, and that
path has a lower activation energy.
The uncatalysed reaction must reach the
higher threshold energy; the catalysed
reaction reaches a lower one.
At the same temperature a much larger
fraction of the molecules has enough
energy for the lower barrier, so many
more collisions form products and the
rate increases.
steps.why: The catalyst does not push the same reaction over the same barrier more quickly. It makes a second route available, and the reaction then runs mostly by that route because its barrier is smaller. That is why the effect is described as a change of path and not a change of speed along one path.
common_mistakes: Writing that the catalyst lowers the energy of the reactants. The reactant and product energies are unchanged; only the peak between them is lowered.
Writing that the catalyst gives the molecules extra energy. It supplies no energy; it reduces how much is needed.
steps.memory_tip: Same start, same finish, lower peak. The path changes, the ends do not.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the lower activation energy, then the larger fraction of molecules that can pass it.

steps.label: What a catalyst does not change
lines: 1. It does not change ΔH of the reaction.
The energies of the reactants and of the
products are the same with and without
the catalyst.
2. It lowers the activation energy of the
forward and of the reverse reaction by
the same amount, so both are speeded
up equally.
3. The equilibrium constant is therefore
unchanged, and so is the yield at
equilibrium.
4. A catalyst only shortens the time taken
to reach equilibrium.
steps.why: The single threshold level is shared by both directions, so lowering it lowers both activation energies by exactly the same amount. Since the equilibrium constant is the ratio of the forward and reverse rate constants, multiplying both by the same factor leaves it unchanged.
common_mistakes: Writing that a catalyst increases the yield of product. It changes only how quickly equilibrium is reached, not where equilibrium lies.
Writing that a catalyst speeds up only the forward reaction. It speeds up both by the same factor.
steps.memory_tip: Sooner, not more. The catalyst changes the time, never the yield.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Points 1 and 3 are the ones examiners look for; number all four.

steps.label: The Arrhenius account
lines: The Arrhenius equation gives the size of
the effect:
Eₐ appears in the exponent with a minus
sign, so lowering Eₐ at a fixed
temperature raises k.
In logarithmic form:
A small drop in Eₐ produces a large rise
in the rate, because the dependence is
exponential and not proportional.
steps.why: The exponential is what makes catalysis worth doing. At 300 K, lowering the activation energy from 100 to 75 kJ mol⁻¹ multiplies k by e^(25000/(8.314 × 300)) = e^10.02, which is about 2 × 10⁴. Lowering the barrier by one quarter gives a rate about twenty thousand times larger.
common_mistakes: Writing k = Ae^(Eₐ/RT) without the minus sign. With a plus sign the equation would say a higher barrier gives a faster reaction.
Saying the catalyst changes A. In this account the frequency factor is treated as unchanged; the effect comes from Eₐ.
steps.memory_tip: Eₐ is in the exponent, so a small drop in it gives a very large rise in k.
steps.margin_note: Two marks: the equation with the correct sign, and the sentence saying why the effect is large.

steps.label: The energy profile
steps.why: The two curves start at the same reactant level and end at the same product level, and only the height of the peak between them differs. That is the whole argument of the answer in one picture: the ends are fixed, so ΔH is fixed, and only the activation energy changes.
common_mistakes: Drawing the catalysed curve ending at a different product level. Both curves must end at the same level, or the diagram claims the catalyst changed ΔH.
Marking only one activation energy arrow. Two arrows to two different peaks are what show the effect.
steps.memory_tip: Two peaks, one start, one finish. The dashed peak is the catalysed path.
steps.margin_note: The question does not say draw, so this earns no marks. All eight sit on the four written steps; sketch it only after they are written.

insider_note: The line that separates a full answer from a half one is that the catalyst does not change ΔH or the equilibrium yield. Write it even if the question only asks about rate.
